interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Toward Auto-Research: Mining Falsifiable Research Ideas from Paper Knowledge Graphs with Categorical Structure
papers.abstract: Automated research-idea generation systems built on large language models (LLMs) share a structural weakness: they reduce ideation to free-text recombination, random paper pairing, or embedding-similarity retrieval. The three approaches fail in the same way: each treats a paper as a flat object, a string or a vector, and so quotients away the typed problem-method-metric-claim arrows a researcher actually uses when reasoning about a cross-domain analogy. We recover the missing structure with the minimal piece of category theory that a typed graph alone does not provide: composition, together with identity arrows, which makes it possible to ask whether a proposed analogy preserves relation chains. Concretely, each paper $p$ is modelled as a small category $C_p$ whose objects are extracted typed research entities and whose morphisms are the relations the paper asserts; a cross-paper bridge from $p$ to $q$ is then a partial functor candidate $F: C_p -> C_q$ that preserves object kinds and covered relation classes. We instantiate the model as a three-layer algorithm: categorical signature clustering, a functor-preservation gate, and a six-axis LLM plausibility judge. Evaluated on a corpus of tens of thousands of full-text-parsed papers under four ablation conditions, the categorical gate filters cross-domain candidates at roughly a 17:1 ratio while the quantitative-falsifier rate of accepted ideas stays above 83% throughout; every rejected candidate is retained with its per-axis rationale, so the gate doubles as a logging layer rather than a silent filter.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper proposes an LLM-based framework for automated research-idea generation using categorical structure in paper knowledge graphs, which aligns with my interest in research agents and automated scientific discovery. The method of preserving typed relations and filtering cross-domain analogies could transfer to astronomy literature mining.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the weakness of LLM-based research-idea generation that treats papers as flat strings or vectors, losing the structured relations researchers use. It introduces a category-theoretic model where each paper is a small category of typed entities and relations, and cross-paper bridges are partial functors preserving structure. A three-layer algorithm filters candidates with a 17:1 ratio while maintaining high falsifiability. For astronomy, this could help generate novel cross-domain research ideas by mining the literature for structured analogies, e.g., between galaxy formation and other fields. One could imagine using it on a corpus of astrophysics papers to propose new hypotheses or connections. However, the approach requires full-text parsing and a well-defined ontology of research entities, which may be a prerequisite to check before applying to astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the categorical structure is defined for astronomy-specific entities (e.g., observations, models, data) or if it is generic
Look for evaluation on a corpus that includes astronomy papers or assess transferability of the method
Inspect the six-axis LLM plausibility judge for any domain-specific calibration or examples

papers.title: CAS: Conformalized Agentic Search via Adaptive Retrieval and Policy Weighting
papers.authors: Zixi Zhu , Jiayuan Su , Jian Zhang , Yu Lin , Hongwei Wang
papers.abstract: Search Agents face a severe reliability crisis during reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning. Heuristic Top-K retrieval often causes critical evidence loss or noise inclusion, while over-confidence induced by progressive RL leads to hallucinated answers and redundant searches. To build highly reliable agents, we introduce Conformal Prediction (CP) and propose Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS). This framework establishes reliability guarantees on both the retrieval and training sides: on the retrieval side, an Adaptive Prediction Set (APS), a specific CP realization, translates statistical coverage into dynamic document truncation to construct prediction sets that are adaptive in size; on the training side, Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI), a dynamic CP algorithm, dynamically constructs prediction sets with controllable coverage to quantify answer confidence, which is then used to penalize low-confidence trajectories within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective, ensuring the model learns only from reliable ones. Experiments across single-hop and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly improves reasoning accuracy while drastically reducing redundant tool invocations, establishing a highly reliable and efficient agent paradigm. Our code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces conformal prediction to improve reliability of search agents, which is directly relevant to retrieval-augmented generation and research agents for astronomy. The methods for adaptive retrieval and confidence-based training could help build more reliable agents for literature search or data analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the reliability crisis in search agents during reinforcement learning fine-tuning, where heuristic retrieval can lose evidence or cause hallucinations. It proposes Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS), which uses conformal prediction to create adaptive prediction sets for retrieval and to penalize low-confidence trajectories during training. This matters for astronomy because it could improve the reliability of LLM-based agents that search astronomical literature or databases, reducing hallucinations and redundant searches. A concrete workflow might be to apply CAS to an agent that retrieves relevant papers or data for a given astronomical query, ensuring the agent only acts on confident evidence. The main caveat is that the method is tested on QA datasets, so one should check if it scales to large astronomical catalogs or multi-modal data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the conformal prediction sets are calibrated on the specific retrieval distribution, which may differ for astronomical text or data.
Look for details on how the adaptive prediction set is constructed and whether it can handle heterogeneous document types.
Assess whether the method requires a reward model or can be applied to existing retrieval pipelines.

papers.title: Decoupled Vision-Language System for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
papers.authors: Yifan Xu , Baochen Xiong , Xiaoshan Yang , Donglin Di , Yaowei Wang , Changsheng Xu
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: We introduce a new architecture design for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Libra, capable of both multimodal understanding and generation. Libra architecture contains one vision system and one language system, connected by cross-modal bridges. This design decouples self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction, enabling each modality to learn its unique representations while maintaining effective cross-modal comprehension. The decoupling is mainly achieved in a switch attention module and a switch FFN module, which dynamically routes the computation flow for self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction scenarios. We evaluate the effectiveness in two important settings: \textbf{Libra-1} for the understanding-only image-to-text setting, and \textbf{Libra-2} for unified image-to-text understanding and text-to-image generation. In addition to the architecture design, we discuss various improvements on tokenization, positional encoding, and supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the dedicated Libra design enables mutual improvements on multimodal understanding and generation, achieving strong performance on both understanding and generation benchmarks.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces a new multimodal LLM architecture (Libra) that decouples vision and language systems, which is relevant to your interest in multimodal models for astronomy. However, it focuses on general image-text tasks, not directly on astronomical data.
papers.Short digest: The paper proposes Libra, a multimodal large language model architecture that separates vision and language processing into distinct systems connected by cross-modal bridges, using switch attention and FFN modules to dynamically route computation. This design aims to improve both multimodal understanding (image-to-text) and generation (text-to-image) by allowing each modality to learn unique representations while maintaining cross-modal interaction. For astronomy, this architecture could potentially be adapted to combine JWST images with spectral or catalog data, though the paper does not demonstrate any astronomical applications. A concrete workflow might involve fine-tuning Libra on astronomical image-caption pairs or using its generation capabilities for synthetic data augmentation. Before investing time, check whether the architecture's tokenization and positional encoding choices are compatible with high-resolution astronomical images and whether the model can handle multi-wavelength or multi-band inputs.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the model supports variable input image sizes or multi-band inputs, which are common in JWST data.
Look for details on the cross-modal bridge mechanism to see if it can be adapted for combining images with spectra or catalogs.
See if the paper provides any analysis of failure modes or limitations when handling complex visual scenes, which could inform astronomical use cases.

papers.title: Tree-of-Concerns: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Debate for Unstated-Limitation Extraction in Scientific Critique
papers.authors: Sahil Mishra , Niranjan Rajeev , Tanmoy Chakraborty
papers.abstract: As scientific literature grows and papers increasingly under-report limitations, multi-agent LLMs offer a promising approach to systematically uncover these hidden failure modes. Here, we introduce Tree-of-Concerns, a multi-agent framework that deploys specialized skeptic personas, each operating through a category-specific analytical lens, as parallel debate trees to extract unstated limitations from scientific papers. Each persona conducts structured, evidence-grounded argumentation, while a Panel Review mechanism re-evaluates each surviving claim from all five perspectives to correct category drift and severity miscalibration. Through experiments on ToC-Bench, our benchmark of 414 research papers with 1,905 unstated limitations, sourced from reviewer-reported weaknesses and follow-up citation critiques, we demonstrate that ToC improves precision by 79% and coverage by 11% relative to strongest baselines, surfacing specific, evidence-grounded concerns that support reviewers in systematic evaluation.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper is about multi-agent LLM debate for extracting unstated limitations in scientific papers, which is relevant to research agents for literature review and scientific critique. The framework could be adapted to help astronomers identify limitations in papers or methods.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether multi-agent LLMs can systematically uncover unstated limitations in scientific papers, which are often under-reported. It introduces Tree-of-Concerns, a framework that deploys specialized skeptic personas in parallel debate trees to extract evidence-grounded limitations, with a Panel Review mechanism to correct category drift. This matters for astronomy because it could help researchers critically evaluate papers or methods, especially in fast-moving fields like JWST analysis. A concrete workflow might be to use this framework to review papers on high-redshift galaxy identification, surfacing potential biases or assumptions. The limitation is that the benchmark is based on reviewer-reported weaknesses, so the method's effectiveness on astronomy-specific papers needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the framework requires a large number of LLM calls, which could be costly for large-scale literature reviews.
Look for details on how the personas are designed and whether they can be customized for astronomy-specific concerns.
Assess if the benchmark includes any astronomy papers or if the method generalizes beyond the tested domains.

papers.title: ForeDreamer: A Self-Evolving Dual-Agent Memory Architecture for Future Event Prediction
papers.authors: Linhao Zhong , Zongze Du , Linyu Wu , Yu Bo , Hourong Li , Chenchen Jing , Hao Chen , Yuling Xi , Chunhua Shen
papers.abstract: Open-web future event prediction requires agents to distill reliable signals from noisy, redundant, and incomplete evidence. Existing retrieval/memory mechanisms directly feed retrieved information to agents or rely on simple memory functions such as storing and reusing prior information for prediction, leaving them insufficient for open-web forecasting. We propose to transform raw web evidence into structured memory before prediction, enabling agents to reason over distilled, question-specific evidence rather than noisy retrieval results. This paper presents ForeDreamer, a self-evolving dual-agent framework for managing memory over open-web evidence. ForeDreamer separates factual memory, a question-specific evidence state for the current forecast, from experiential memory, persistent agent experience accumulated across forecasting episodes. It uses a main agent for search and prediction, and a memory-processing subagent to convert search results into factual memory with dedicated tools. ForeDreamer further evolves experiential memory through two tracks, improving both forecasting decisions and factual-memory construction. Experiments on Prophet Arena and FutureX demonstrate the effectiveness of ForeDreamer. Project page: this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces a dual-agent memory architecture for future event prediction from open-web evidence, which could transfer to research agents for literature review or data analysis in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper presents ForeDreamer, a self-evolving dual-agent framework for future event prediction from noisy web evidence. It separates factual memory (question-specific evidence) from experiential memory (persistent agent experience) and uses a main agent for search and prediction with a memory-processing subagent. This could matter for astronomy if one builds agents to predict transient events or synthesize literature, but the paper is not astronomy-specific. A concrete workflow might be using such an agent to gather and reason over astronomical literature or alerts, but it requires adaptation. A limitation is that it is evaluated on general forecasting benchmarks, not scientific data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the memory architecture can handle domain-specific evidence like astronomical catalogs.
Look for any discussion on adapting to scientific workflows.
